missing_important: OpenMC's MOAB unstructured-mesh tallies accept only linear tetrahedra: MOABMesh warns 'Non-tetrahedral elements found in unstructured mesh file' if the 3D range is not all MBTET (openmc src/mesh.cpp:3149-3153) and the install docs say the MOAB option 'allows unstructured mesh tallies on tetrahedral MOAB meshes' (docs/source/usersguide/install.rst:317). DAGMC itself consumes only triangles. So MOAB's first-class polyhedra, mixed elements and high-order nodes have zero downstream leverage in the neutron-transport ecosystem today; this weakens the 'h5m as interchange export' lesson for a polyhedral-first mesher unless the transport code is written to read it.

OpenMC geometry docs, verbatim: 'DAGMC geometries used in OpenMC are currently required to be clean, meaning that all surfaces have been imprinted and merged successfully and that the model is watertight. Future implementations of DAGMC geometry will support small volume overlaps and un-merged surfaces.' (docs/source/usersguide/geometry.rst:530-536). DAGMC ships overlap_check and make_watertight tools (src/overlap_check, src/make_watertight). Tolerating overlaps / un-merged (non-conformal) surfaces is a stated roadmap item, not a feature.

OpenMC's DAGMC surface boundary conditions (src/dagmc.cpp:448-476): only transmit/transmission, vacuum, and reflective/reflect/reflecting are accepted; 'periodic' hits fatal_error('Periodic boundary condition not supported in DAGMC.'); any other string (e.g. 'white') is an 'Unknown boundary condition' fatal error; graveyard-bounding surfaces are forced to VacuumBC.

Coreform Cubit already ships the DAGMC/h5m exporter the project would need to match: 'export dagmc <filename> [faceting_tolerance <tol>] [length_tolerance <tol>] [normal_tolerance <tol>]' (DAGMC doc/usersguide/cubit_basics.rst:105-107, cubit_workflow.rst:62). Per svalinn/Cubit-plugin README and Coreform's 2023.11 release note, the plugin has been bundled since Cubit 2023.8 and DAGMC export is native since 2023.11. DAGMC docs still describe it as 'the Cubit plugin'.

h5m carries no format-version attribute. The only provenance is the `history` dataset of (application, version, date, time) strings appended per write (mhdf.h:91-106); c_h5mformat.h defines no version field. This confirms the report's 'version the on-disk spec' as a genuine differentiator rather than an assumption.

MOAB has a structured-mesh interface (ScdInterface/ScdBox) that stores structured blocks without explicit connectivity and exposes block parameters as set tags (doc/details/b_iometadata.h:128), and NestedRefine/umr provides a uniform (non-adaptive) refinement hierarchy with no hanging nodes. The report omits both; the first matters for lattice/pin-cell reactor geometry, the second reinforces that MOAB has no non-conformal representation.

Geometry-set ordering nuance: GEOM_DIMENSION sets are unordered except EDGE (curve) sets, where 'order of the mesh vertices and edges corresponds to the relative order of vertices and edges at the time of mesh generation' (b_iometadata.h:65). Curves are the one place MOAB preserves a parametric-like ordering; surfaces/volumes get none.
MOAB is built as C++14 (CMakeLists.txt:3-4: CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14), confirming the 'pre-C++17' characterization. PR #681 (5.6.0) also deprecated mbcslam alongside ITAPS/iMesh and the CGM links.

summary: DMPlex is PETSc's unstructured-mesh DM. It stores topology as a Hasse diagram (a DAG of integer "points" with cone/support covering relations), derived from Knepley and Karpeev's Sieve. Fields are laid out by PetscSection, parallelism by PetscSF, and subsets by DMLabel. It is a mature, widely used topology plus data-layout layer in PETSc (docs checked here are release 3.26.0). It is dimension-agnostic and cell-shape-agnostic at the topology level. Non-conformity is handled by a side "tree" structure and by DMForest/p4est (Isaac and Knepley, arXiv:1508.02470). It is a library data model with a versioned HDF5 storage format (parallel format 3.0.0), not a standalone interchange spec. Several details are only partly verified, and the unverified items are marked in the fields below.
data_model: Topology: every entity (cell, face, edge, vertex) is a "point", a PetscInt in a contiguous chart [pStart, pEnd) set with DMPlexSetChart. The mesh is a covering relation: an edge is covered by 2 vertices, a triangle by 3 edges. The cone holds the in-edges of the DAG (what covers a point). The support is the dual relation. Cones are ordered and carry orientation; supports are not ordered. Build sequence: DMPlexSetConeSize, DMSetUp, DMPlexSetCone, DMPlexSymmetrize (supports from cones), DMPlexStratify (depth/height indices). Query API: DMPlexGetCone, GetSupport, GetTransitiveClosure (cone or support direction, breadth-first order), GetJoin/GetMeet and GetFullJoin/GetFullMeet (for example, find a face from its vertices), GetDepthStratum and GetHeightStratum. Storage is CSR-like: a cone-size/offset array plus a concatenated cones array, with an orientation array parallel to the cones (the DMPlexCreateFromDAG signature takes coneSize, cones and coneOrientations). Point numbering is by stratum. The manual's 2D example numbers cells, then vertices, then edges, and says 3D is cells, vertices, faces, edges, which is the height-0 first convention. Interpolation (DMPlexInterpolate, as a creation option in DMPlexCreateFromCellListPetsc) creates the intermediate edges and faces from a cells-to-vertices mesh. Entry points: DMPlexCreateFromCellListPetsc (cells to vertices, only process 0 reads input) and DMPlexCreateFromDAG (explicit DAG: depth, numPoints[depth+1], coneSize, cones, coneOrientations, vertexCoords). Orientation: integer orientation numbers map to the dihedral-group permutations of the cone through PetscSectionSym. 0 is canonical and a negative value means reversed. Cell type is recorded per point as a DMPolytopeType, normally in a label (the "celltype" label name is from memory and unverified). Data: PetscSection maps point to (offset, ndof) and defines the local/global layout; DMSetField with PetscFE and DMCreateDS build the sections. Vectors are indexed through the section, and DMPlexVecGetClosure gathers the values over a point's closure (ordered field, closure point, dof). Geometry: coordinates are a vertex field with a section, and DMLocalizeCoordinates gives a cell-wise coordinate field for periodicity. Sources: https://petsc.org/release/manual/dmplex/ , https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/DMPlex/DMPlexCreateFromDAG/ , https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/DMPlex/DMPlexCreateFromCellListPetsc/
polyhedra: Topologically the Hasse diagram allows any cone size, so an arbitrary polygon or polyhedron can be stored as a point whose cone is its faces (cell, then face, then edge, then vertex) with no fixed-shape assumption. The DMPolytopeType enum lists only fixed types: POINT, SEGMENT, TRIANGLE, QUADRILATERAL, TETRAHEDRON, HEXAHEDRON, PYRAMID, TRI_PRISM, the tensor types (POINT_PRISM_TENSOR, SEG_PRISM_TENSOR, TRI_PRISM_TENSOR, QUAD_PRISM_TENSOR), the ghost types (FV_GHOST, INTERIOR_GHOST) and UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN_CELL, UNKNOWN_FACE. Source: https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/DM/DMPolytopeType/ . The page names no general-polyhedron type, so arbitrary polyhedra fall under UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN_CELL. Per the DMPolytopeType page, the type must sometimes be user-specified when interpolating from cell-vertex input, because the polytope can be ambiguous. Whether geometry (volume, centroid) and FE/FV closure routines work on UNKNOWN cells is unverified. I believe finite-volume geometry (DMPlexComputeCellGeometryFVM) handles general polyhedra via face triangulation, but I did not verify this. FEM discretization needs a reference element, so it is effectively limited to the listed shapes.
nonconformal: Native DMPlex is a conformal CW-complex: two faces are either the same point or distinct. Non-conformity is added through a "tree". Isaac and Knepley (arXiv:1508.02470) record subset/superset relations between entities in a tree structure that is separate from the DAG. The docs say so explicitly for DMPlexGetTreeChildren: the tree is "not the DAG". The API is DMPlexSetTree, DMPlexGetTree, DMPlexGetTreeParent and DMPlexGetTreeChildren. Reference trees describe the possible types of non-conforming interface. Hanging-node constraints are computed internally, so FE code written for conformal meshes extends automatically. Only the abstract of the paper was readable. The PDF fetch failed, so the internal data structures (the anchor section and the constraint matrix) are unverified. For adaptive refinement, DMFOREST (with p4est as the first backend) holds a forest refined from a base DMPLEX. DMForestSetBaseDM says the base "must be a DMPLEX" for now. The forest is converted to a DMPlex with the tree structure for the solver. Detection is by construction: non-conformity comes from the refinement hierarchy, not from geometric matching of independent meshes. There is no imprinting or detection step, and I found no mortar/projection support for arbitrarily mismatched, independently meshed interfaces. That absence is unverified. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.02470 , https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/DMForest/DMForestSetBaseDM/ , https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/DMPlex/DMPlexGetTreeChildren/ , https://lists.mcs.anl.gov/pipermail/petsc-users/2019-September/039437.html
sets_and_partitions: Labels (DMLabel) hold point to integer value, and a value acts as a stratum (a set of points). They are used for depth, cell type, boundary markers and region/material IDs. Exact label names ("depth", "celltype", "Face Sets", "Cell Sets") come from my memory of Exodus/Gmsh readers and are unverified here, and the DMLabel manual page returned 404. Labels are saved by DMPlexLabelsView and are used by the adaptors, which take boundary and interior labels to preserve (DMAdaptMetric). A material layer is just another label, and there is no first-class layered model of geometry, partition and mesh. Parallel: DMPlexDistribute(dm, overlap, &sfDist, &distDM) partitions the mesh. The graph partitioned is the mesh itself, and the result is returned as IS objects. A PetscSF (star forest) maps old points to new ones, and SFs compose (PetscSFCompose) across load and distribute. The overlap argument defaults to 0. Adjacency is configured separately with DMSetAdjacency using useCone and useClosure (FEM uses cone=false, closure=true; FVM the opposite). Ghost points are created by overlap. The doc page did not describe the overlap semantics, so those details are unverified. Sources: https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/DMPlex/DMPlexDistribute/ , https://petsc.org/release/manual/dmplex/
strengths: Dimension- and shape-agnostic topology: one integer DAG with cones, supports and closures. Algorithms (closure, join/meet, adjacency) are generic across dimensions.
Cleanly separates topology (DAG), data layout (PetscSection), parallel communication (PetscSF) and subsets (DMLabel), so new fields and ghosting come for free.
Database-like queries: closure, star, join/meet, strata by depth and height, labels as indexed subsets.
Parallel is first-class: SF-based distribution and overlap, and parallel HDF5 with load on a different process count.
Handles hanging nodes and AMR through the tree and p4est, with automatic constraint handling. Supports metric adaptation via Pragmatic, Mmg and ParMmg.
Built-in orientation algebra (dihedral-group permutations) and reordering and permutation of closures.
Mature and long-lived, with many importers (Gmsh, Exodus, CGNS, med per my memory, unverified).
weaknesses: Only integer point IDs with no stable entity identity: numbering changes under distribution and reordering, with a separate global numbering saved alongside.
The format is a library dump rather than an independent, formally specified interchange standard, and it is tied to PETSc's HDF5 versioning.
No first-class polyhedron type, and the fixed polytope enum is FE-oriented.
Non-conformity exists only through refinement trees. There is no general mismatched-interface (imprint or mortar) representation.
High order and curved geometry are handled through coordinate fields and sections rather than a dedicated cell-level high-order spec.
No link to CAD/B-rep geometry in the core model, beyond labels.
Heavy dependency on PETSc and C, and the API is low-level and stateful (SetChart, SetConeSize, SetUp, SetCone, Symmetrize, Stratify).
Face-set and material semantics are conventions in label names rather than schema.
lessons_for_us: Adopt: model the mesh as a DAG of entities (cone and support) with a CSR layout plus an orientation array. This is one uniform representation for polyhedra, mixed cells and any dimension. Keep a cell-type tag, but make 'arbitrary polyhedron = cell whose cone is its faces' the base case.

Adopt: keep sections (entity to dof layout), labels (entity to value sets) and the topology as independent layers, joined only by entity IDs. This maps naturally onto the geometry, partition and mesh layers.
Adopt: build supports and strata as derived, rebuildable indices from the cones. Keep cones as the single source of truth.
Adopt: represent distribution as an explicit star-forest-like mapping (local to remote ID) that composes, instead of baking ghosting into the topology.

Differ: use stable global entity IDs (for example 64-bit or UUID-like) carried through every operation instead of positional integer points. This helps traceability, incremental edits and CAD association.
Differ: make geometry association first-class by giving each mesh entity an optional owning B-rep entity reference and a parametric location. PETSc has only labels.

Differ: represent non-conformal interfaces explicitly as a typed relation. A subset or superset tree covers the refinement case, and a separate 'imprint/mortar' relation links two geometrically overlapping faces that are not identical. Store the overlap polygons so a solver can project without re-detecting.

Differ: ship a formal, versioned, language-neutral schema (for example Arrow or HDF5 plus a spec) instead of a library-defined dump. Take the PETSc HDF5 hint that strata are stored per depth with cone_sizes, cones and orientations as arrays.
Differ: give polyhedra, high-order nodes and material/region sets schema-level types instead of naming conventions.
sources: https://fluid.colorado.edu/source/raw/petsc/src/dm/impls/plex/hdf5/plexhdf5.c (fetch timed out; layout taken from the manual)
database_like_aspects: The DAG is essentially a relational model with two inverse relations (cone and support). Closure, star, join and meet are graph queries over it. Strata by depth and height act as typed indexes. DMLabel is a secondary index (value to point set). PetscSection acts as a column store keyed by point. DMPlexSymmetrize and DMPlexStratify build derived indexes from the primary cone relation. Adjacency is computed on demand from a (useCone, useClosure) policy instead of being stored. There is no declarative query language or transactions, and the schema is implicit.
ecosystem: PETSc, with direct users in libMesh-adjacent FE codes, PyLith (per my memory, unverified), the TS/SNES FEM/FVM examples, and the Firedrake and ex-Fluidity ecosystems (per my memory, unverified). Importers: the manual pages and the Gmsh/Exodus/CGNS importers are from my memory and unverified. Bindings: C, Fortran, Python through petsc4py. Output: HDF5 with an XDMF companion for ParaView (unverified). Adaptation: Pragmatic, Mmg and ParMmg.
geometry_association: None to B-rep in the core. Geometry association is by labels (boundary and region IDs) and a coordinate field. The metric adaptors take boundary and interior labels to preserve. Mmg and the surface meshers do not support surface remeshing (the docs say surface meshing is not supported). I found no CAD-entity reference in DMPlex itself, but I did not search the full source for one, so treat that as unverified.
high_order: There is no dedicated high-order cell type in the topology. Topology stays linear (vertices, edges, faces, cells), and high order is a function-space matter: PetscSection assigns dofs per point (the manual's P3 example gives 1 dof per cell, 1 per vertex, 2 per edge) and DMPlexVecGetClosure gathers them using the orientation permutations. Curved geometry uses a coordinate field of higher degree through DMSetCoordinateDisc (unverified; I did not fetch that page). Edge orientation flips the dof order along edges.
parallel: DMPlexDistribute(dm, overlap, &sfDist, &distDM) redistributes the mesh and returns a PetscSF from the old to the new points, and NULL if no distribution is needed. Partitioning works on the mesh graph itself and returns IS objects. The overlap argument defaults to 0 and sets how much overlap partitions have. DMSetAdjacency controls the (useCone, useClosure) policy that decides the overlap and matrix coupling. Ghost points are part of the local DAG, with SF roots and leaves defining ownership. HDF5 format 3.0.0 is parallel and is enabled with -dm_plex_view_hdf5_storage_version 3.0.0. It supports loading on a different process count than saving, and it stores global point numbers with the mesh so sections and vectors can be matched after reload. Sources: https://petsc.org/release/manual/dmplex/ , https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/DMPlex/DMPlexDistribute/
spec_quality: Weak as an interchange spec. The HDF5 layout is documented in the manual only in outline (format 3.0.0: strata stored in groups 0 to 3, each with cone_sizes, cones and orientations). It is versioned by a (major, minor, sub) triple through PetscViewerHDF5Set/GetDMPlexStorageVersionReading and Writing. It is defined in plexhdf5.c rather than a standalone spec document, and the full group and dataset naming is unverified because the source fetch timed out. The API documentation is good, but the data model is implicit in code.
storage: HDF5 through PETSc viewers. DMView calls DMPlexTopologyView, DMPlexCoordinatesView and DMPlexLabelsView. Sections and vectors go through DMPlexSectionView and DMPlexLocalVectorView. Version 3.0.0 is parallel, and storage versions are set separately for reading and writing, with -dm_plex_view_hdf5_storage_version as the override. Strata are stored as groups with integer arrays, which suits parallel collective I/O. I have no benchmark data on performance, which is unverified.

corrections.claim: geometry_association: "None to B-rep in the core. Geometry association is by labels and a coordinate field"; weakness "No link to CAD/B-rep geometry in the core model, beyond labels"; lesson "PETSc has only labels".
corrections.correction: DMPlex ships an optional CAD layer (src/dm/impls/plex/plexegads.c, EGADS/EGADSlite). DMPlexCreateGeomFromFile(comm, filename, &dm, islite) reads EGADS, IGES, STEP (DMPlexCreateFromFile dispatches .egads/.egadslite/.igs/.iges/.stp/.step/.brep to it). The B-rep model is attached to the DM as a PetscContainer ("EGADS Model", "EGADS Context") and every mesh point is tagged with labels "EGADS Body ID", "EGADS Face ID", "EGADS Edge ID", "EGADS Vertex ID". Parametric location is available (DMPlexGetGeomModelTUV: t on edges, (u,v) on faces). DMSnapToGeomModel(dm, p, dE, mcoords, gcoords) is called inside DMPlexTransformSetCoordinates, so vertices created by refinement snap to the CAD surface; DMPlexInflateToGeomModel (XYZ or TUV mode) re-projects drifted vertices; DMPlexGeomDataAndGrads/DMPlexModifyGeomModel expose control points and shape-optimization gradients (-dm_plex_geom_shape_opt). Caveats: EGADS is the only DMSnapToGeomModel implementation; it is an optional external package; the initial mesh is only an EGADS surface tessellation (no volume mesher). Reword the 'Differ' lesson: PETSc already has entity-ID + parametric CAD association, but it is EGADS-bound and encoded as label conventions rather than schema.

corrections.claim: "I believe finite-volume geometry (DMPlexComputeCellGeometryFVM) handles general polyhedra via face triangulation".
corrections.correction: DMPlexComputeGeometryFVM_3D_Internal does fan-triangulate faces, but it enumerates faces through DMPlexGetRawFaces_Internal(dm, ct, ...) keyed on DMPolytopeType, which handles only POINT..PYRAMID and errors "No face description for cell type %s" for UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN_CELL. Face handling accepts only triangles and quadrilaterals ("Cannot handle face %d of type %s"), and pyramid is an open TODO ("DO FOR PYRAMID"). So FV geometry does not work for arbitrary polyhedra.

corrections.claim: "arbitrary polyhedra fall under UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN_CELL" (presented as a usable fallback) and "Whether geometry and FE/FV closure routines work on UNKNOWN cells is unverified".
corrections.correction: Polyhedra can be stored only via DMPlexCreateFromDAG with explicit cones; essentially every consumer then fails. DMPlexComputeCellType_Internal infers type from (dim, cone size) with default -> DM_POLYTOPE_UNKNOWN, and DMPlexComputeCellTypes (triggered automatically the first time a cell type is requested) raises PETSC_ERR_SUP "Point %d has invalid celltype (%s)" for UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN_CELL/UNKNOWN_FACE. DMPlexTransformSetUp (all refinement/extrusion) errors "No cell type for point %d". DMPlexInterpolate rejects "faces of size > 4". The CGNS reader rejects NGON_n/NFACE_n. The manual's sentence that residual code "will work for polyhedral cells" refers only to closure-based data access, not geometry, interpolation, refinement or discretization. Net: no first-class polyhedron support; the report's 'Adopt: polyhedron as base case' is a genuine differentiator, not an adoption from PETSc.

corrections.claim: Importers include "med per my memory, unverified".
corrections.correction: DMPlexCreateFromFile (release) has no MED reader. Dispatch by extension: .msh/.msh2/.msh4 -> Gmsh; .cgns -> CGNS; .exo/.e/.gen -> ExodusII; .cas -> Fluent; .h5 (or .xdmf.h5) -> HDF5 DMLoad; .ply -> PLY; .egadslite/.egads/.igs/.iges/.stp/.step/.brep -> CAD (EGADS); .dat -> cell-vertex; .stl -> STL; .shp -> Shapefile; otherwise "Cannot load file %s: unrecognized extension".

corrections.claim: "the DMLabel manual page returned 404"; label names "celltype", "Face Sets", "Cell Sets" are "from my memory and unverified".
corrections.correction: Wrong URL; the page exists at manualpages/DM/DMLabel/ ("Object which encapsulates a subset of the mesh from a DM"). Label names are confirmed: DMPlexGetCellTypeLabel/DMPlexComputeCellTypes create an internal label named "celltype"; the Gmsh reader creates "Cell Sets", "Face Sets", "Edge Sets" (dim>2), "Vertex Sets" and, with -dm_plex_gmsh_use_regions, labels named after $PhysicalNames.

corrections.claim: "integer orientation numbers map to the dihedral-group permutations of the cone through PetscSectionSym. 0 is canonical and a negative value means reversed."
corrections.correction: Orientation indexes the symmetry group of the point's polytope type (dihedral only for polygons; tets/hexes have 24/48 arrangements). Docs: "Orientation 0 is always the identity transformation. Negative orientation indicates reflection so that -(o+1) is the reflection of o, however it is not necessarily the inverse" (use DMPolytopeTypeComposeOrientationInv). Cone permutations come from DMPolytopeTypeGetArrangement/ComposeOrientation; PetscSectionSym is the dof-permutation layer, not the encoding.

corrections.claim: HDF5 "strata are stored in groups 0 to 3, each with cone_sizes, cones and orientations"; "parallel format 3.0.0" as the versioning anchor.
corrections.correction: 3.0.0 layout is /topologies/<name>/topology/permutation plus /topologies/<name>/topology/strata/<depth>/{cone_sizes,cones,orientations}; labels under /topologies/<name>/labels/<label>/<value>/indices; sections/vecs under /topologies/<name>/dms/<dm>/... The full version list in plexhdf5.c is 1.0.0, 1.1.0, 2.0.0 (adds topologies/ hierarchy), 2.1.0 (adds distributions/<name>/{chart_sizes, owners, global_point_numbers}, which is where the 'global point numbers' live), 3.0.0 (strata/permutation, parallel; "Since PETSc 3.19"), 3.1.0 (IS compression only). Default write version DMPLEX_STORAGE_VERSION_STABLE = "1.0.0" (legacy serial); LATEST = "3.1.0"; parallel is opt-in via -dm_plex_view_hdf5_storage_version 3.0.0.

corrections.claim: Ecosystem: "direct users in libMesh-adjacent FE codes".
corrections.correction: libMesh has its own mesh class and does not use DMPlex. Confirmed DMPlex users: Firedrake (Lange, Mitchell, Knepley, Gorman, SISC 2016), PyLith (mesh held in DMPlex, developer docs), Ratel/libCEED (JOSS 2026). Drop 'libMesh-adjacent'.

corrections.claim: "Mmg and the surface meshers do not support surface remeshing (the docs say surface meshing is not supported)".
corrections.correction: DMAdaptMetric's page says nothing about surface meshing; it only documents bdLabel/rgLabel preservation. Adaptors pragmatic|mmg|parmmg are confirmed via -dm_adaptor. Remove or mark as unverified.

corrections.claim: "Output: HDF5 with an XDMF companion for ParaView (unverified)".
corrections.correction: True only for the legacy/VIZ layout: lib/petsc/bin/petsc_gen_xdmf.py reads /viz/topology/cells or /topology/cells, /geometry/vertices, /vertex_fields, /cell_fields (cell-vertex arrays). It does not read the 3.0.0 DAG strata checkpoint. PETSc itself therefore keeps a separate viz export (PETSC_VIEWER_HDF5_XDMF/VIZ, VTK, CGNS) from its checkpoint format, a point relevant to the IR-vs-export discussion.

missing_important: Non-conformal: the tree API is verified (DMPlexSetTree(dm, parentSection, parents, childIDs): 'a point is constrained to the points in the closure of its tree root'; DMPlexSetReferenceTree; DMPlexCreateDefaultReferenceTree(comm, dim, simplex) = isotropic hierarchical refinement, i.e. 2:1 hanging nodes for simplex or tensor cells). Underneath sits a GENERAL mechanism the report missed: DMPlexSetAnchors(anchorSection, anchorIS) + DMGetDefaultConstraints define point-to-point constraints where a point's dofs are 'a linear combination of other points' degrees of freedom'. PETSc only auto-fills that matrix from reference trees, but it is exactly the hook where mortar/mismatched-interface coupling would be injected. No detection/imprinting of independently meshed interfaces exists (confirmed absent from docs and source searched).

Interfaces as cells: DMPlexCreateHybridMesh(dm, label, bdlabel, bdvalue, ...) inserts zero-thickness cohesive ('hybrid') cells along a labeled internal surface, duplicating the surface points; DMPlexTransform type 'cohesive_extrude' does the same; the *_PRISM_TENSOR enum entries exist for these cells (PyLith faults). This is PETSc's model of an internal interface and is directly relevant to the user's partition/interface layer.

DMPlexTransform framework (not mentioned): refine_regular, refine_alfeld, refine_powell_sabin, refine_boundary_layer, refine_sbr, refine_tobox, refine_tosimplex, refine_1d, extrude, cohesive_extrude, transform_filter. All require known cell types (DMPlexTransformSetUp errors on UNKNOWN).

High-order I/O exists and is parallel: plexcgns2.c implements a parallel CGNS reader (cgp_*, -dm_plex_cgns_parallel, limited to one base/one zone) and a parallel CGNS writer (DMView_PlexCGNS) that writes coordinates at the field's Lagrange order; full Lagrange orders 1-4 are mapped (TETRA_10, HEXA_27, HEXA_64, ...); serendipity and NGON_n/NFACE_n are rejected. The Gmsh reader supports MSH 2.2/4.0/4.1 (v3 rejected), curved high-order coordinates (-dm_plex_gmsh_highorder, default on for order>1, not for hybrid meshes), -dm_plex_gmsh_periodic, -dm_plex_gmsh_project. DMSetCoordinateDisc(dm, disc, localized, project) exists; note 'the discontinuous coordinates are not updated' when projecting.

Point numbering is a convention, not a requirement: the manual's convention is 3D cells, vertices, faces, edges (2D: faces, vertices, edges), but DMPlexCreateFromDAG numbers 'all points consecutively' by depth starting at vertices (example numPoints=[4 2]). Only per-stratum contiguity is needed.
DMPlexCreateFromCellListPetsc takes input 'only on process 0'; DMPlexCreateFromCellListParallelPetsc / DMPlexBuildFromCellListParallel exist for distributed input (used by the parallel CGNS reader).

Version/status confirmed: docs are PETSc 3.26.0 (released Sep 28, 2026; 3.25 Mar 30, 2026; 3.24 Sep 29, 2025). DMForestSetBaseDM: 'Currently the base DM must be a DMPLEX' confirmed. DMPlexDistribute(dm, overlap, &sf, &dmParallel) confirmed; overlap is documented only as 'the width of the cell overlap' (layers of cells under the DMSetAdjacency policy).

topic: Sandia STK Mesh (Sierra ToolKit, Trilinos) and Omega_h
summary: STK Mesh is the mesh database of Sandia's Sierra mechanics codes, shipped as the stk_mesh package in Trilinos and used externally by Nalu(-Wind) and Panzer/STK. It is an in-memory, mutable, parallel entity database. Entities are typed by rank (node, edge, face, element, and others) and carry part memberships. Entities with identical part membership are grouped into homogeneous Buckets, and fields are stored per bucket. Parts, Selectors and Fields are separate layers over one entity set. That is close to the user's "geometry / partition / mesh coexist" model and to the "mesh as database" view. STK is not a file format. I/O goes through Exodus (stk_io) and its spec is its C++ headers. Omega_h (SNL/Sandia Labs, FreeBSD license) is a much smaller GPU-oriented library for tri/tet adaptation, built on flat CSR-like arrays plus tags. I fetched the STK headers and Omega_h headers from GitHub master/main. The Nalu docs page and the Omega_h README were fetched as web pages. FleCSI and the Kokkos-device NgpMesh internals were not examined and are unverified. Several remarks on STK internals (bucket-per-part-signature rule, Exodus-centric I/O) come from reading header comments and field names, not from a formal spec.
data_model: STK. EntityKey is a 64-bit value: rank in the top 8 bits (RANK_SHIFT = 56), id in the low 56 bits (EntityKey.hpp). Ranks are stk::topology::NODE_RANK, EDGE_RANK, ELEMENT_RANK. Face/side rank is looked up via metaData.side_rank() (Nalu docs). MetaData holds the schema (parts, fields, side rank). BulkData holds the entities, buckets, relations and ghosting. An Entity is a lightweight handle, an index into BulkData internal tables. Bucket (Bucket.hpp) is a homogeneous std::vector<Entity> m_entities with m_size, m_capacity and m_maxCapacity (default capacities set by get_default_bucket_capacity()). It has a std::vector<unsigned> m_key, the sorted list of part ordinals shared by all its entities, and an impl::Partition* m_partition. Buckets also carry ngp_mesh_bucket_id and ngp_field_bucket_id plus "modified" flags used for host-to-device (Kokkos NgpMesh/DeviceMesh) syncing. Connectivity is stored per bucket in BucketConnectivity<TargetRank, ConnectivityType> (BucketConnectivity.hpp). The Bucket has m_node_kind, m_edge_kind and m_face_kind, each FIXED or DYNAMIC. The FIXED variant holds m_targets as a flat vector<Entity> indexed bucket_ordinal*m_num_connectivity, plus m_ordinals (ConnectivityOrdinal, local position/slot) and m_permutations (orientation, not stored for node targets). So an element bucket of one topology stores a dense N-per-entity table. Both downward and upward relations are materialized, per the Nalu docs: bulk.begin_nodes(elem), num_nodes(elem). The older Relation objects are being replaced by this per-bucket connectivity (my reading; unverified as a formal statement). Fields: declare_field<T>(rank, name, numStates), put_field_on_mesh(field, part, nComponents, init) which defines a FieldRestriction by (rank, part) and so ties storage to part membership. field_data(field, bucket) returns a flat pointer with stride per entity (av[k*nDim+j]). Multi-state fields use field_of_state(StateN / StateNP1 / StateNM1). The newer FieldData.hpp/FieldDataBase.hpp provide typed accessors, and DeviceField/HostField provide Kokkos mirrors. Omega_h. Mesh holds, per dimension 0..3, a set of tags (named arrays with ncomps, add_tag(dim,name,ncomps,Read<T>)). Adjacency is a struct Adj : Graph with a2ab (CSR offsets, absent when fixed-arity), ab2b (CSR targets) and Read<I8> codes (an encoded rotation and orientation of the sub-entity). Downward adjacencies are the stored ones (e.g. element to vertices, via set_ents(dim, down)). Upward ones come from invert_adj and are derived and cached on demand through ask_up, ask_down and derive_adj, held in shared_ptr<const Adj>. Classification is stored as tags (class_dim, class_id), and ClassSets is map<string, vector<ClassPair{dim,id}>> for named sets. Arrays are Read<T>/Write<T> device-aware, ref-counted. Parallel info: Remotes owners_[dim] and a global id array per dimension (Omega_h_mesh.hpp). It has an Omega_h_Family enum (simplex or hypercube, set_family).
polyhedra: STK: entities are typed by stk::topology, not only by rank. Standard topologies cover the usual shapes, and arbitrary-node-count shapes are supported in some form (topology has superelement and particle-style types; unverified for general polyhedra). Because connectivity is typed FIXED or DYNAMIC per bucket, a bucket with a variable count of faces/nodes per entity could use DYNAMIC. I did not verify any general polyhedral support (face-based polyhedron with arbitrary face counts) in STK. Omega_h: only simplex and hypercube families (Omega_h_Family); no polyhedra.
nonconformal: Not verified, and not a first-class concept in what I read. STK's mesh is topologically conformal by construction: entities are connected via shared nodes/sides. Sierra's contact and mortar-style tie handling is done by separate search and contact libraries (stk_search, stk_transfer, stk_middle_mesh) operating on surface parts, not by a non-conformal flag in the database. That is an inference from the package layout and is unverified. Omega_h: conformal only.
sets_and_partitions: STK Parts are the key feature for us. A Part is "an application-defined subset of a problem domain" (Part.hpp). It has a name, mesh_meta_data_ordinal, primary_entity_rank, and a DAG of supersets()/subsets() (add_part_to_subset/superset). Membership is stored per entity as a sorted ordinal list; entities with identical lists live in the same Bucket (m_key). So element blocks, sidesets, nodesets, "locally owned", "shared" and "active" are all just Parts. Selector (Selector.hpp) is a boolean expression tree over Parts with &, |, - and ! (complement). get_buckets(rank, selector) evaluates it per bucket key rather than per entity, which makes queries cheap. A Part can induce membership downward (e.g. element in block puts its nodes in it; Part::should_induce). Fields are attached to parts via restrictions. A single entity can be in many parts at once, which handles multiple coexisting partitions. Omega_h: classification tags and ClassSets (named list of (dim,id) model entities) tie mesh entities to geometric model entities; no general part mechanism.
high_order: STK: topologies include higher-order variants for tet/hex/etc. (e.g. TET_10, HEX_27), so high-order here means Lagrange nodes stored as extra nodes in the element-to-node table. Arbitrary p is not supported. Details unverified beyond the topology naming. Omega_h: linear only for the cavity operations, with P2 fields discussed elsewhere (unverified).
parallel: STK: each entity has an owning rank. Elements are owned by a single rank and may be ghosted. Nodes/faces/edges on the partition boundary are shared among all ranks that touch them, and the lowest rank owns (Nalu docs). Ghosting (Ghosting.hpp) is a named, user-definable object: it holds the owned entities ghosted elsewhere (send) and entities ghosted here (receive). Built-in aura ghosting exists, and custom ghostings can be added. The communication state lives in EntityCommDatabase. Field parallel ops are in FieldParallel (parallel_sum, communicate, etc.). Mesh modification uses a collective modification_begin/modification_end cycle that resolves ownership and sharing. Omega_h: Remotes owners_[dim] (rank,index) per entity, a global-id array per dimension, sync_array/reduce_array/owned_array for exchange; output is deterministic and independent of partitioning (README).
database_like_aspects: STK is the closest thing to "mesh as database" among the codes I examined. There is an explicit schema (MetaData: parts, fields, ranks), separate from instance data (BulkData). Entities are rows with a 64-bit key, i.e. a primary key with type. Part membership is a set-valued attribute and Selector is a query predicate (boolean algebra over sets) evaluated by bucket. Buckets are a physical clustering index by part signature, and also work as a column-store layout for fields (SoA by bucket, same-length rows). Relations are materialized in both directions. Mesh modification happens in transactions (modification_begin/end). Omega_h is database-like in a different way: dimension-indexed tables (one per entity dimension) with named columns (tags), and adjacency indexes (CSR) derived on demand and cached, so it is a relational-style design with lazy materialized views.
geometry_association: STK: no B-rep link inside the core. Association with geometry is done only through Parts (block/sideset ids from Exodus). Omega_h: classification is first class. Each mesh entity has class_dim and class_id tags pointing at a model entity; ClassSets groups them by name. This is the SCOREC/PUMI convention of geometric classification (verified in Omega_h_mesh.hpp).
ecosystem: STK: Sierra/SM, SD, Aria etc. (internal at Sandia, unverified list), Trilinos-based Nalu and Nalu-Wind (ExaWind), Panzer (via panzer_stk). I/O is Exodus through stk_io and IOSS (Ioss). C++ only, with Kokkos for the device mesh/fields (DeviceMesh.hpp, DeviceField.hpp). Omega_h: C++, MPI/OpenMP/CUDA, optional Exodus (Omega_h_USE_SEACASExodus), and its own binary format. Used in the Sandia Albany/Trilinos ecosystem (unverified). No Python or Rust bindings noticed.
spec_quality: No formal spec for STK. The reference is the Doxygen-documented C++ headers, which change between Trilinos releases (e.g. Bucket.hpp has deprecated field_data_location marked "Delete after September 2025"). The Part/Selector semantics are clear in header comments. Omega_h likewise has no file or data-model spec; its README does not describe the mesh data model.
storage: STK: in-memory only; persistence via Exodus II (NetCDF/HDF5). Bucket capacity bounded (default/maximum bucket capacity functions) to keep cache-sized chunks. Fixed connectivity is a dense array (entity-major, N-per-entity) while dynamic connectivity is used otherwise (CSR-like details unverified). Omega_h: flat device-aware arrays, plus optional zlib-compressed binary files (README mentions ZLib as preferred; format not examined).
strengths: Parts + Selectors give a clean, composable partition layer (materials, blocks, sidesets, ownership flags) that is orthogonal to rank and topology; one entity can be in many parts
Bucket by part signature makes selector queries and field storage cheap and gives homogeneous loops (single topology per bucket allows vectorized kernels)
Explicit MetaData/BulkData split is a real schema/instance split and fields are declared against (rank, part), so layout is derived from partition
Entity key encodes rank and id in 64 bits; ghosting is a first-class, named object
Omega_h shows that adjacency as CSR/graph with an orientation code per edge, derived lazily and cached, is a compact GPU-friendly design
Omega_h classification (dim, id) is a simple robust geometry link
weaknesses: STK is large, C++ heavy, with a steep learning curve and no standalone spec or on-disk format, so it cannot serve as an interchange IR
Rank-centric model (node/edge/face/element) assumes conformal, mostly Exodus-like meshes; polyhedra and non-conformal faces are not first class (not verified as absent)
Mutating a part membership moves the entity between buckets, which is costly; bucket churn under adaptivity
Face rank is not a fixed constant (side_rank depends on dimension), which complicates dimension-independent code
Omega_h supports only simplex/hypercube and has no part mechanism, no polyhedra and no non-conformal support
lessons_for_us: Adopt: separate schema (parts, fields, ranks) from instance data, as MetaData vs BulkData. It gives a database feel and makes the IR self-describing

Adopt: partitions (material/color/region) as named sets with a subset/superset DAG, and queries as a boolean Selector algebra evaluated on set signatures, not on entities. This directly models the user's second layer (conceptual partition, not geometry)
Adopt: group cells by (topology, part-signature) into buckets for homogeneous SoA data and fast selection, but make bucket membership a derived index, not part of the stable on-disk format
Adopt from Omega_h: CSR adjacency (offsets + targets + orientation code), downward stored, upward derived and cached on demand; store only what is minimal
Adopt from Omega_h/PUMI: classification = (dim, id) pointer from each mesh entity to a B-rep entity; this is the geometry layer link
Adopt: 64-bit key with rank in the high bits and id in low bits is a simple stable id scheme
Differ: make polyhedral cells (face-based: cell to faces to nodes with orientation) the primary representation and treat standard topologies as an optimization; STK is topology-first

Differ: represent non-conformal interfaces explicitly as a face-pair (or face-patch) relation between two unmatched faces with a declared tolerance/mapping, instead of leaving it to external search/contact libraries
Differ: define a versioned, language-neutral on-disk spec (STK has none) so the IR is an interchange format and not just an in-memory library
Differ: avoid entity movement between buckets on part changes; keep membership as a separate bitset/CSR column and rebuild bucket indexes lazily
Open question to verify before design: how STK's DYNAMIC connectivity and polyhedral topologies work in practice, and whether stk_middle_mesh or stk_search offer a non-conformal model

corrections.claim: Ranks are stk::topology::NODE_RANK, EDGE_RANK, ELEMENT_RANK. Face/side rank is looked up via metaData.side_rank().
corrections.correction: stk::topology::rank_t (int8_t) defines NODE_RANK, EDGE_RANK, FACE_RANK, ELEM_RANK (=ELEMENT_RANK) and CONSTRAINT_RANK as fixed constants; MetaData additionally accepts user-defined extra rank names (MetaData(spatial_dim, rank_names) / initialize(...)). side_rank() only selects among them by spatial dimension: NODE_RANK (1D), EDGE_RANK (2D), FACE_RANK (3D). EntityKey reserves 8 bits for rank (RANK_SHIFT=56ULL, MAX_ID=2^56-1, id 0 invalid) - confirmed.
corrections.source: stk_topology/topology_decl.hpp lines 30-37; stk_mesh/base/MetaData.hpp lines 158, 326-339, 345-351; EntityKey.hpp lines 49-60

corrections.claim: Entities with identical part membership live in the same Bucket (m_key); buckets are a physical clustering index by part signature.
corrections.correction: Grouping is by impl::Partition, keyed by the sorted part-ordinal list (m_extPartitionKey). A Partition owns one or more Buckets (BucketVector m_buckets) of bounded capacity (get_default_initial_bucket_capacity / get_default_maximum_bucket_capacity), so one part signature normally spans several buckets. Each Bucket also has exactly one stk::topology (m_topology). Partition::move_to/add/remove are the entity-movement operations.

corrections.claim: put_field_on_mesh(field, part, nComponents, init) defines a FieldRestriction by (rank, part) and so ties storage to part membership.
corrections.correction: FieldRestriction holds a Selector (m_selector), not a Part: it can be constructed from a Part or from an arbitrary Selector expression, and restrictions are unioned (add_union). put_field_on_mesh has Part and Selector overloads. So field layout is derived from a selector predicate over parts, which is slightly more general than the report states.

corrections.claim: Dynamic connectivity is used otherwise (CSR-like details unverified).
corrections.correction: Now verified: impl::BucketConnDynamic stores a per-entity IndexRange {first,second} offset pair (m_offsets) into flat m_connectivity / m_ordinals / m_permutations arrays with a compression threshold, i.e. a mutable CSR-with-slack layout. Upward element connectivity in a bucket (m_dynamic_element_connectivity) is ALWAYS dynamic; only downward node/edge/face connectivity can be FIXED (BucketConnectivity<Rank, FIXED_CONNECTIVITY>, dense bucket_ordinal*m_num_connectivity, ordinals shared 0..N-1). The report's statement that the legacy Relation class is 'being replaced' remains unverified: Relation.hpp still exists on master with no deprecation marker, and BulkData still uses RelationIdentifier/RelationVector internally.

corrections.claim: Arbitrary-node-count shapes are supported in some form (superelement and particle-style types; unverified for general polyhedra). I did not verify any general polyhedral support in STK.
corrections.correction: Resolved: STK has NO polyhedron topology. stk::topology::topology_t contains no POLYHEDRON/NSIDED/NFACED entry (grep 'poly' finds nothing). SUPEREDGE/SUPERFACE/SUPERELEMENT topologies are pure node-bags: topology_data<SUPERELEMENT_START+n> inherits topology_data<INVALID_TOPOLOGY>, defines only num_nodes=n, rank=ELEMENT_RANK and side_rank=INVALID_RANK, with no vertices/edges/faces/permutations, so a face-based polyhedral cell cannot be expressed. stk_io's map_ioss_topology_to_stk only maps aliasable named topologies plus names starting with 'super' (-> create_superelement_topology(num_nodes)); everything else returns INVALID_TOPOLOGY. Exodus nsided/nfaced (polyhedral) element blocks therefore have no STK topology to land on (the exact error/skip behaviour on import was not traced). The 'unknown' handling in IossBridge is for heterogeneous sidesets, not polyhedra.

corrections.claim: Sierra's contact and mortar-style tie handling is done by separate search and contact libraries (stk_search, stk_transfer, stk_middle_mesh) ... inference from package layout and unverified.
corrections.correction: Now verified and more specific. stk_middle_mesh is a sibling package (with stk_middle_mesh_util) that computes a 'middle grid' (common refinement / supermesh) between two non-matching surface meshes: ApplicationInterface::create_middle_grid(), get_middle_grid_for_mesh1()/mesh2(), get_mesh1_classification()/get_mesh2_classification() (middle-grid element -> parent element on each side), compute_mesh*_inverse_classification() (parent -> middle-grid elements), and get_xi_points_on_mesh1()/mesh2() (parametric coords of middle-mesh points on each side). It uses its own lightweight tri/quad mesh class with GeoClassification, a 'nonconformal4' normal-projection algorithm with explicit tolerances (PointClassifierNormalWrapperTolerances, EdgeTracerTolerances), and parallel search via stk_search. Nothing non-conformal is stored in stk_mesh BulkData itself. Nalu (and Nalu-Wind) instead handle non-conformal/sliding interfaces purely at solve time: a DG-like penalty flux with the opposing element found by a parallel search per integration point ('A parallel search is conducted to project the current integration point location to the opposing element exposed face'), and 'The full connectivity for element integration and opposing elements is within the linear system'. So the ecosystem baseline is: core = conformal only; non-conformal = either a computed supermesh with two-way classification maps (stk_middle_mesh) or algorithm-level search each step (Nalu).
corrections.source: packages/stk/stk_middle_mesh/stk_middle_mesh/application_interface.hpp lines 77-136; mesh.hpp; nonconformal4_opts.hpp; packages/stk directory listing (GitHub API); https://nalu.readthedocs.io/en/latest/source/theory/boundaryConditions.html#non-conformal-boundary-condition

corrections.claim: Omega_h: conformal only.
corrections.correction: The simplex adaptation path is conformal, but Omega_h ships an amr module (Omega_h_amr.hpp/.cpp) for hierarchical, non-conformal (hanging-node) refinement of hypercube meshes: Mesh stores Parents/Children relations (set_parents, parents_[DIMS], children_[DIMS][DIMS], Parents{parent_idx, codes}, Children: Graph with codes encoding which_child|parent_dim), leaf flags (ask_leaves), amr::refine/derefine, enforce_2to1_refine (2:1 balance across a bridge dimension) and remove_non_leaf_uses. amr.cpp asserts hypercube_split_degree, i.e. hypercube family only.

missing_important: STK stores sidesets twice: as Parts on side entities AND as explicit Exodus-style stk::mesh::SideSet objects per surface Part, i.e. vectors of SideSetEntry{Entity element; ConnectivityOrdinal side} (BulkData::create_sideset/get_sideset/does_sideset_exist, SideSet::add(elem, side), set_accept_all_internal_non_coincident_entries). An (element, local-side-ordinal) pair representation of boundaries is thus first-class alongside face entities; relevant to the IR's boundary-set design. (SideSetEntry.hpp lines 51-149; BulkData.hpp lines 821-829)

STK keeps a face-adjacent element-to-element graph (ElemElemGraph, BulkData::get_face_adjacent_element_graph()) plus utilities skin_mesh, create_edges, create_faces, declare_element_side; cell-to-cell adjacency across sides is a maintained derived structure, not recomputed ad hoc. (BulkData.hpp lines 86-87, 131-133, 354, 809-810)

Selector nodes are of type PART or FIELD (SelectorNodeType), so a selector can also select buckets where a given field is defined; operators are union |, intersection &, difference -, complement ! as the report says. (Selector.hpp lines 53-196)

Part carries an int64 id() (Exodus block/sideset id), an optional topology(), force_no_induce and entity_membership_is_parallel_consistent flags; should_induce(from_rank) == (primary_entity_rank()==from_rank && !force_no_induce()). Confirmed as the report describes. (Part.hpp lines 96-138)

The stk package family on Trilinos master: stk_balance (parallel partitioning/rebalance, incl. Zoltan2-based), stk_coupling (code-to-code coupling), stk_emend, stk_expreval, stk_io, stk_math, stk_mesh, stk_middle_mesh(+_util), stk_search(+_util), stk_simd, stk_tools, stk_topology, stk_transfer(+_util), stk_util, plus a hip_porting directory and AGENTS.md. (GitHub API contents of packages/stk)

Nalu docs confirm the parallel ownership rule the report cites: elements owned by a single rank; exposed faces, nodes, edges and internal faces are owned by the lower parallel rank and shared by all touching ranks; custom ghosting is used for elements. STK's aura is configurable via BulkData::AutomaticAuraOption {NO_AUTO_AURA, AUTO_AURA} and aura_ghosting(). (nalu codeAbstractions page; BulkData.hpp lines 161-200, 549)

stk::mesh::Entity is a handle holding a local_offset (uint32 or uint64 by build) into BulkData tables; the header states local_offset generally remains unchanged through modification cycles, so offsets may be non-compact. (Entity.hpp lines 63-85)

Omega_h is single-family per mesh: enum Omega_h_Family {OMEGA_H_SIMPLEX, OMEGA_H_HYPERCUBE} with no mixed option, and the README limits adaptation to triangles/tetrahedra while emphasising fully deterministic, partition-independent results. Omega_h also offers reorder_by_hilbert / reorder_by_globals for locality. (Omega_h_defines.hpp line 69; README lines 36-48; Omega_h_mesh.hpp lines 192-193)

Omega_h can link directly to a B-rep via EGADS (Omega_h_USE_EGADS, 'Use EGADS from ESP for geometry'), so its classification (dim,id) can point at real CAD model entities, not just integer labels. (CMakeLists.txt line 23)

summary: The Mesh Blueprint is a convention (schema plus verify/transform library) layered on LLNL's Conduit, a hierarchical in-memory tree of named nodes holding typed arrays. A mesh is a Conduit tree with sections coordsets, topologies, matsets, specsets, fields, nestsets, adjsets and state. A multi-domain mesh is an Object of such trees. It acts as an in-memory interchange IR between simulation codes and Ascent, VisIt, MFEM, VTK-m and Silo. Conduit is actively maintained: latest release found is 0.9.9 (2026-09-30), and Blueprint gained mixed-shape and polyhedral support in partition()/iterate_elements() in 0.9.5. It is a convention checked by verify() functions, not a formal versioned standard. Several gaps matter for us (see weaknesses): no winding spec, no nonconformal support, minimal high-order, and no geometry/B-rep link. Evidence is from the official docs, the GitHub releases page and web search snippets. I did not read the source code or the Ascent/VisIt docs (the Ascent URL I tried returned 404), so Ascent/VisIt usage statements rest on the Blueprint docs and release notes only.
data_model: Container: a Conduit Node tree (path-addressed, e.g. topologies/topo/elements/connectivity). Leaves are typed arrays. An 'mcarray' (multi-component array) can be stored interleaved, as separate component arrays, or strided, and the schema also allows offsets/strides. Coordsets: 'uniform' (dims/{i,j,k}, origin, spacing), 'rectilinear' (values/{x,y,z}), 'explicit' (values mcarray). Coordinate systems: Cartesian {x,y,z}, cylindrical {z,r}, spherical {r,theta,phi}. Topologies: each has a 'coordset' reference. Implicit types: points, uniform, rectilinear, structured (elements/dims/{i,j,k}, elements/origin), and strided structured (elements/dims/offsets and strides, selecting a sub-block of the coordset). Explicit type 'unstructured' uses elements/shape plus elements/connectivity. Shapes: point, line, tri, quad, tet, hex, pyramid, wedge, polygonal, polyhedral, mixed. Fixed-size shapes need only connectivity (vertex indices per shape count). Polygonal uses connectivity 'end to end' plus elements/sizes and elements/offsets (a one-to-many relation, o2mrelation: sizes, offsets, optional indices). Mixed: elements/shape='mixed' with shape_map (name to numeric id, which are VTK type ids, e.g. hex=12, tet=10, polyhedron=42, quad=9, tri=5, polygonal=7), shapes (one numeric id per element), sizes, offsets and connectivity. Fields: fields/<name> with association ('vertex' or 'element'), topology, values (mcarray), optional volume_dependent, offsets, strides. A field can instead use 'grid_function'/basis, the name of an MFEM-style finite-element collection (the docs show it both as a topology-level 'grid_function' reference and as a field key that replaces association), or matset+matset_values for material-dependent data. There is no first-class edge or face entity and no stored cell-to-cell adjacency; relations are derived on demand by library functions (e.g. generate_* utilities). State: time, cycle, domain_id, level_id. A Mesh Index (blueprint_index/<mesh>/{coordsets,topologies,fields,state}, plus file_pattern, number_of_files, tree_pattern, protocol/name and version) lets a reader discover a multi-file dataset without loading the data.
polyhedra: First class. elements/shape='polyhedral' has elements/connectivity, sizes and offsets that index into a sibling 'subelements' node (shape='polygonal', with its own connectivity, sizes, offsets), whose connectivity indexes coordset vertices. So the layout is cell to face to vertex (an explicit two-level o2m), where faces are stored once per cell reference in the list; the docs state 'There is no assumed ordering for constituent polyhedral faces relative to their source polyhedra' and I did not find a statement of face orientation/outward normal rules (unverified). In a 'mixed' topology, 'subelements' is only needed if polyhedra are present. Tooling: partition() handles polyhedra and mixed shapes (0.9.5), the partitioner reverses vertex order in polyhedral faces as needed (0.9.2), combining no longer duplicates faces (0.9.1), convert() turns polyhedral hex meshes into unstructured hex (0.9.6), to_polygonal()/to_polytopal exist. Examples: basic('polyhedra'), polytess, polychain.
nonconformal: No first-class support found. The nesting sets section (nestsets) covers AMR parent/child relations only for structured topologies and states unstructured is not yet supported. Nestset windows have association, topology, windows/<w>/{domain_id, domain_type ('parent' or 'child'), ratio/{i,j,k}, origin/{i,j,k}, dims/{i,j,k}}, and each domain needs state/level_id. The docs page has no mention of hanging nodes or non-conforming interfaces; the only trace is a 0.9.6 release-note item about MPI to_polygonal transferring 'vertex data on hanging nodes' (from the releases page, I did not confirm the context). Adjacency sets (adjsets) describe inter-domain shared vertices/elements for conforming partition boundaries, not mortar/mismatched faces. A non-conformal interface would have to be inferred by geometry or modeled outside the schema (e.g. as a custom field or a separate topology). Detection is by convention, not by schema.
sets_and_partitions: Materials: matsets are bound to a topology and have four layouts. (1) Multi-buffer element-dominant: volume_fractions is an Object keyed by material name, dense, optional material_map. (2) Multi-buffer material-dominant: volume_fractions and element_ids both Objects keyed by material, sparse. (3) Uni-buffer element-dominant: material_map, material_ids, volume_fractions arrays, with optional sizes/offsets/indices (an o2mrelation from element to its materials), sparse. (4) Uni-buffer material-dominant (element_ids): documented as not currently supported. Material ids are arbitrary unique integers. Library: conversions between layouts (to_multi_buffer_by_element, to_uni_buffer_by_element, to_multi_buffer_by_material; to_uni_buffer_by_material throws), to_silo (matlist, mix_next, mix_mat, mix_vf), renumber_material_ids, MatsetAccessor, has_mixed_elements (0.9.8), partitioner handles matset_values (0.9.7). Specsets: matset + matset_values (mcarray organized material then species). Mixed (partial-volume) cells are handled via volume fractions only; there is no interface-reconstruction geometry in the schema. There is NO general named entity-set / boundary-set / element-block concept; the idiom is to encode regions as integer-valued fields or as additional topologies (e.g. a boundary topology of lower dimension referencing the same coordset, which I believe is the common convention but did not verify as normative). Parallel: a multi-domain mesh is an Object of domains; adjsets (association vertex or element, topology, groups/<g>/{neighbors, values}) in pairwise or max-share variants; group names must match across domains and utils::adjset::canonicalize assigns matching names. Ghost layers have no dedicated schema element that I found (unverified). Nothing in the docs links layers (geometry, partition, mesh) beyond reference-by-name strings.
strengths: Genuinely used as a lingua franca: Ascent, VisIt, MFEM and VTK-m are documented as consumers/producers, and the winding page names them.
Zero-copy, language-neutral tree with typed arrays; C++, Python, Fortran bindings; I/O via Conduit Relay (HDF5, ADIOS, YAML/JSON) per the broader Conduit project (not re-checked here).
Schema is data (paths and arrays), so adding an optional section or field is cheap and independent of code; verify() functions give schema validation.
Rich multi-material model: four layouts, sparse/dense, species sets, conversions and Silo bridge, partitioner awareness.

Coordsets and topologies are separate and reference-by-name, so several topologies can share one coordset (a boundary mesh or sub-mesh without duplicating points); implicit structured/uniform/rectilinear avoid storing connectivity.
Polyhedra and mixed shapes are first class and the partition/convert/generate tooling is maintained (0.9.x series, 0.9.9 on 2026-09-30).
Mesh Index plus multi-domain model supports scalable multi-file parallel datasets and cheap discovery.
o2mrelation (sizes, offsets, indices) is a single reusable pattern for every ragged relation.
weaknesses: Not a formal spec: the docs say no winding convention is prescribed (VTK assumed), no face/edge cascade, no polyhedral face ordering or orientation rule I could find.

High-order is essentially absent in the schema: only an MFEM collection name in 'grid_function'/basis fields; no Lagrange/Bernstein node ordering, no curved-geometry definition, and no topology-level element order key found.
Non-conformal and hanging-node meshes are not representable in the schema; nestsets are structured-only; adjsets assume conforming partition boundaries.
No intrinsic faces, edges or adjacency, so face-based solvers (finite volume, DG, transport) must derive and cache them; no boundary-condition or sideset concept.
No named sets or blocks, no geometry-association layer (no B-rep, no entity-to-CAD links), no versioned history/provenance.
Mixed topologies use VTK numeric ids in shape_map, which ties the IR to VTK ids; the docs also contain typos in the mixed example (coordset vs type), suggesting loose spec hygiene.
Per-element sparse material layouts and the unsupported material-dominant uni-buffer variant show incomplete coverage.
Documentation-defined, not machine-readable schema (no JSON Schema/IDL); validation lives in C++ code.
Chiefly an in-memory/in-situ exchange layer; on-disk performance depends on Relay backends and was not benchmarked here.
lessons_for_us: Adopt: separate coordset (points) from topology (cells) from fields, with cross-references by name; allow several topologies over one coordset (volume mesh, boundary mesh, interface mesh) without duplicating points.
Adopt: one universal ragged-relation primitive (sizes, offsets, optional indices) for every one-to-many link: cell to vertices, cell to faces, face to vertices, set to members, element to materials.

Adopt: path-addressed, typed-array tree with zero-copy views as the logical model, with a Mesh Index (cheap header) so tools can navigate without loading bulk arrays; this fits the user's 'zoom out with minimal context' idea too.

Adopt: multi-layer separation like matsets (partition layer) as a first-class object referencing a topology, but go further: make 'region/material/boundary set' a general named-set entity (entity dimension + member list + attributes) rather than only volume fractions.

Deliberately differ: make faces and edges first-class stored (or lazily materialized and cached) entities with face-to-cell (left/right) incidence and explicit orientation rules, because a transport/DG consumer needs face-based adjacency; Blueprint leaves this to utilities.

Deliberately differ: write a normative spec (winding, face orientation, node ordering, units, versioning, machine-readable schema such as JSON Schema or FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto) instead of 'VTK is assumed'.

Deliberately differ: add non-conformal interface as a first-class object (interface pairs of face sets with mortar/projection metadata and an 'imprinted vs not-imprinted' flag), plus hanging-node/parent-child relations for unstructured meshes; Blueprint's nestsets are structured-only.

Deliberately differ: add a geometry-association layer (each mesh entity carries a link to a B-rep entity id and parametric coords) and keep geometry, partition and mesh layers as separate graph nodes with typed edges.
Deliberately differ: specify high-order explicitly (basis family, order per element, node ordering, geometry order) instead of delegating to an MFEM collection name.

Adopt: provide a Blueprint-compatible export/adapter (and VTK/Exodus/CGNS/MFEM exporters) rather than chasing format parity; use the partitioner/verify design (verify, convert, partition, generate_*) as a model for an IR transformation API.
Adopt: mirror Blueprint's multi-domain plus adjset idea for parallel, but include ghost layers and a global-id map explicitly, with matching group names enforced by a canonicalize step.
database_like_aspects: Strongly database-like in being a self-describing tree: named tables-of-arrays (coordsets, topologies, fields, matsets) cross-referenced by name (topology.coordset, field.topology, matset.topology, adjset.topology) like foreign keys. Ragged relations are CSR-style (sizes, offsets, indices). Verify functions act like schema constraints, and the Mesh Index is like a catalog. Missing database features: no queries/indices beyond library functions, no derived adjacency stored, no transactions or versioning, no named-entity-set tables.
geometry_association: None in the Blueprint schema. There is no link from mesh entities to CAD/B-rep entities; region or boundary identity is conventionally carried by integer fields or extra topologies, which I did not verify as normative.
high_order: Minimal. The only support is a field-level 'grid_function'/basis key holding an MFEM-style finite element collection name (replacing 'association'), plus an optional topology-level reference to a grid_function field; no Lagrange or Bernstein node ordering, no per-element order, no curved-geometry description found in the docs I read. Higher-order meshes in practice are handled via MFEM interop (details unverified).
ecosystem: Conduit (C++, Python, Fortran bindings) with Relay I/O; Blueprint mesh is the data interface of Ascent (in-situ visualization), consumed by VisIt, MFEM and VTK-m (the docs say these assume VTK winding). It has Silo conversion (to_silo) and also an MPI-parallel layer (conduit::blueprint::mpi::mesh, e.g. generate_index, partition). Releases: current 0.9.9 on 2026-09-30. I could not load the Ascent docs page (404), so the extent of Ascent/VisIt features such as polyhedra rendering is unverified.
parallel: Multi-domain meshes are Objects of domains, each carrying state/domain_id. Adjacency sets (association vertex or element; groups/<g>/{neighbors, values}) in pairwise or max-share variants with matching group names across domains and canonicalize(). MPI utilities include generate_index, partition (with targets and selections), and 0.9.x improved partitioning for mixed/polyhedral/matset meshes. AMR is handled by nestsets (structured only). Ghost layers have no dedicated schema element that I found (unverified).
storage: Conduit Relay writes/reads the tree to HDF5, ADIOS, YAML/JSON, and Silo (via to_silo and conversions), per the general Conduit project; the details are unverified in this session. Performance characteristics: zero-copy in-memory views, typed contiguous arrays with offsets/strides; the Mesh Index (blueprint_index with file_pattern, number_of_files, tree_pattern) supports multi-file datasets. No benchmarks were reviewed.
spec_quality: Medium to low as a standard: the docs page is a human-readable protocol description with a version of Conduit (0.9.9) but I found no separately versioned Blueprint spec number (the protocol/version "0.4.0" in the docs is only the example mesh index value). Strengths: a verify() function per section and a rich examples generator (basic, braid, spiral, julia, venn, polytess, polychain, tiled). Weaknesses: winding and cascade explicitly unspecified, no polyhedral face orientation rule, minimal high-order, typos in the mixed example, no machine-readable schema.

corrections.claim: Polyhedral layout is cell-to-face-to-vertex 'where faces are stored once per cell reference in the list'.
corrections.correction: `subelements` is a shared face table, not a per-cell face list. The docs' own polyhedral example has `elements/connectivity: [0,1,2,3,4, 0,5,6,7,8]` with `sizes: [5,5]`: face 0 (`[1,2,4,3]`) is referenced by both polyhedra. Face sharing is corroborated by the 0.9.1 note ('partitioner ... does not duplicate faces when combining polyhedral meshes') and the 0.9.2 note ('reverses vertex order as needed in polyhedral face definitions'). Design consequence: a shared face has exactly one stored vertex order, so the schema structurally cannot carry an outward-normal orientation for both adjacent cells; the only normative statement is 'There is no assumed ordering for constituent polyhedral faces relative to their source polyhedra.' (A ParaView discourse thread makes the same complaint; the 0.9.2 fix shows the library compensates implicitly, it is not a spec rule.)

corrections.claim: Mixed topologies: shape_map maps name to numeric id, 'which are VTK type ids'.
corrections.correction: The spec only gives VTK ids as examples ('e.g. 12 - VTK_HEXAHEDRON'); numerically the ids are publisher-defined. But every checked consumer enforces VTK ids: Ascent's adapter calls `CheckShapeMapVsViskoresShapeIds()` and raises `ASCENT_ERROR("Shape Map Entries do not match required Viskores Shape Ids.")` if they differ; VisIt's adaptor compares `shapes` values directly against `VTK_POLYHEDRON`/`VTK_POLYGON`. So the correct framing is 'spec permits arbitrary ids, ecosystem requires VTK ids' — which strengthens the report's weakness.

corrections.claim: High-order: 'the only support is a field-level grid_function/basis key holding an MFEM-style finite element collection name (replacing association)'; docs show grid_function 'as a field key that replaces association'.
corrections.correction: Two different keys at two levels: `fields/<f>/basis` (mfem-style FE collection name) is the FIELD key that replaces `association`; `topologies/<t>/grid_function` is a TOPOLOGY key naming the field that holds the (possibly curved/high-order) mesh nodes. MFEM's ConduitDataCollection confirms the pattern: `n_topo["grid_function"] = "mesh_nodes"`, `fields/mesh_nodes/basis = FESpace()->FEColl()->Name()`. Node ordering is therefore delegated entirely to MFEM's FiniteElementCollection semantics; VisIt (needs an MFEM build) and Ascent (`refinement_level`, Devil Ray) reconstruct an mfem::Mesh and refine to low order for visualization.
corrections.source: blueprint_mesh.rst lines ~200 and ~1268; https://docs.mfem.org/4.8/conduitdatacollection_8cpp_source.html; visit avtBlueprintFileFormat.C (MFEM LOR); https://ascent.readthedocs.io/en/stable/AscentAPI.html

corrections.claim: Non-conformal: 'the only trace is a 0.9.6 release-note item about MPI to_polygonal transferring vertex data on hanging nodes'.
corrections.correction: Blueprint has an established idiom for hanging nodes that the report missed: degenerate to polytopes. `blueprint::mpi::mesh::to_polygonal` (v0.8.0, 2021-12) is documented as 'conversion Blueprint Structured AMR meshes to a Blueprint Polyhedral meshes', with `to_polytopal`/`to_polyhedral` aliases; the `polystar` example (v0.8.3) 'creates a mesh with a polyhedral star pattern that demonstrates hanging vertices in a topology'; 0.9.6 added field transfer 'including communication of vertex data on hanging nodes'. I.e. a hanging node becomes an extra vertex of the coarse polygon/polyhedron, making the mesh topologically conformal. The report's core conclusion stands: there is no mortar/interface/projection object, and nestsets are structured-only (verbatim: 'currently only supports nesting specifications for structured topologies').

corrections.claim: 'The docs also contain typos in the mixed example (coordset vs type), suggesting loose spec hygiene.'
corrections.correction: True of the v0.9.5 docs (mixed schema listed `topologies/topo/coordset: "unstructured"`), fixed in the latest docs (`topologies/topo/type: "unstructured"`). It was in the schema key list, not a YAML example.

corrections.claim: 'Blueprint gained mixed-shape and polyhedral support in partition()/iterate_elements() in 0.9.5' (presented as the arrival of mixed/polyhedral support).
corrections.correction: 0.9.5 (2025-09-10) only extended two tooling functions. Schema support is much older: o2mrelation-based polygonal/polyhedral since v0.6.0 (2020-11-02), `mixed` shape protocol since v0.8.4 (2022-08-22), `partition()` since v0.8.0 (2021-12-20), nestsets verify since v0.4.0. Release dates confirmed: 0.9.6 2026-04-14, 0.9.7 2026-05-27, 0.9.8 2026-09-01, 0.9.9 2026-09-30 (latest).

corrections.claim: 'I could not load the Ascent docs page (404), so the extent of Ascent/VisIt features such as polyhedra rendering is unverified.'
corrections.correction: Ascent docs are live at ascent.readthedocs.io (AscentAPI, Tutorial_Intro_Conduit_Blueprint). Resolved from source: Ascent's main (Viskores/VTK-m) runtime does NOT accept polyhedral or polygonal Blueprint topologies: the unstructured path supports only tri, quad, tet, hex, points, wedge, pyramid (`ASCENT_ERROR("Unsupported element shape ")`), and its mixed path's reference shape map has no polyhedron/polygon entry. VisIt does accept polyhedral/polygonal (it runs `generate_sides` to decompose them, auto-generates missing offsets, handles mixed-with-polyhedra by splitting, but rejects mixed polygonal+polyhedral in one topology). VTK/ParaView Catalyst2 (`vtkConduitToDataObject`) supports polyhedral and mixed via `SetPolyhedralCells` (copying faces per cell), except on its Viskores path ('Viskores does not support VTK_POLYHEDRON cell type').

corrections.claim: Polyhedral: 'elements/shape=polyhedral has elements/connectivity, sizes and offsets'; polygonal 'uses connectivity end to end plus elements/sizes and elements/offsets'.
corrections.correction: Correct in practice, but note the docs' polyhedral schema listing shows only `elements/connectivity` and `subelements/connectivity`; `sizes`/`offsets` appear only in the example. VisIt's reader source states 'Polyhedral meshes require offsets to verify' and generates them before `verify()`, so offsets are effectively mandatory. (Also: `generate_offsets`/`generate_offsets_inline` exist for this.)
corrections.source: blueprint_mesh.rst polyhedral schema; visit avtBlueprintFileFormat.C GenerateOffsetsForPolytopalMesh

missing_important: Ghost-layer convention (code-derived, not in the Blueprint spec): Ascent option `ghost_field_name` / `ghost_field_names` (default element field `ascent_ghosts`); values 0 = real, 1 = ghost, 2 = garbage (runtime comment 'garbage zones have a value of 2'; it thresholds [0,1] then strips to [0,0] for rendering). ParaView Catalyst2 instead uses `state/metadata/vtk_fields/<field>/attribute_type: "Ghosts"` (plus `values_to_replace`/`replacement_values`) to map onto `vtkGhostType`. Two consumers, two incompatible ghost encodings — a concrete reason to make ghost/ownership a first-class field in your IR.

Ecosystem reach omitted: ParaView Catalyst 2 uses Conduit as its ABI and the Mesh Blueprint as the data protocol for its `mesh` and `multimesh` channels; VTK ships IO/CatalystConduit (vtkConduitSource/vtkConduitToDataObject) with polyhedral and mixed support. Together with Ascent, VisIt, MFEM (ConduitDataCollection) and Axom Sidre, Blueprint is the de facto in-situ interchange across both LLNL and Kitware stacks — so a Blueprint exporter buys visualization in Ascent, VisIt and ParaView at once (with the Ascent polyhedra caveat above). Ascent's backend is now 'Viskores' (VTK-m successor).

Database-relevant: Conduit also defines a Table Blueprint (`values` of equal-length columns/mcarrays, 'easily translated to and from CSV') and `blueprint::mesh::flatten()` (v0.8.0) converts a Blueprint mesh into Blueprint Tables (point/element tables). This is a direct precedent for the user's 'mesh as a database' framing.

Derived incidence exists even if not stored: `generate_points/lines/faces/centroids/sides/corners` (serial and MPI) all return `s2dmap`/`d2smap` source<->destination maps, so face->cell incidence is obtainable from a generated face topology; `topology::unstructured::iterate_elements()` (0.9.5) walks mixed/polyhedral elements; `convert()` (0.9.6) converts among topology types ('structured, rectilinear, unstructured, generate_lines, ...').

Boundary/region-set convention now confirmed rather than believed: MFEM's ConduitDataCollection writes the boundary as a separate lower-dimensional topology (referenced by a non-standard `boundary_topology` key) plus integer element fields `element_attribute` and `boundary_attribute`; Blueprint's `related_boundary` example (v0.8.3) 'creates a multi-domain mesh with a related boundary topology and several fields that encode relationships between the main topology and the boundary'. There is still no named-set object in the schema.

Winding/cascade statement verbatim: 'The mesh blueprint does yet not have a prescribed winding convention ... or more generally to outline a topology's dimensional cascade ... with a goal of providing transforms to help convert between different winding or cascade schemes'; and the shape table note says the authors 'are not likely to specify specific orderings'. So the gap is deliberate policy, not an omission to be fixed upstream.

Matset detail: 0.9.6 removed the multi-buffer matset indirection variant (children of `volume_fractions` can no longer be o2mrelations); Ascent's adapter also rejects material-dominant uni-buffer matsets and o2mrelation `indices` for matsets, so only the simplest layouts are portable.
Ascent coordset limits: its adapter accepts only Cartesian {x,y,(z)} and 2D cylindrical {r,z}; spherical and 3D cylindrical coordsets error out despite being in the Blueprint spec.
Mesh Index also carries `number_of_trees` and `tree_pattern`; VisIt requires a root file (hdf5/json/yaml) to open Blueprint data.

topic: VTK family: VTU/PVTU, VTKHDF, XDMF, ADIOS2/Fides/VTX as mesh interchange formats
summary: The VTK family is a visualization-oriented data model (vtkUnstructuredGrid: points plus a flat cell array plus per-cell type ids) with several serializations. These are legacy .vtk, XML .vtu/.pvtu, the HDF5-based VTKHDF (spec version 2.8 per docs.vtk.org, community-governed, covers PolyData, UnstructuredGrid, ImageData, RectilinearGrid, StructuredGrid, HyperTreeGrid, Table, OverlappingAMR, MultiBlock and PartitionedDataSetCollection), and XDMF (an XML light-data description pointing at HDF5 heavy data). ADIOS2 with Fides and VTX is a separate streaming and HPC-IO route, where a JSON schema maps ADIOS variables to a dataset. All of it is widely read by ParaView and VisIt. It is a de facto interchange and visualization format, not a simulation-grade mesh IR. Polyhedra are supported in VTU/VTKHDF through an auxiliary face structure. Fides appears not to support polyhedra. Non-conformal interfaces, CAD association and sets are not first-class anywhere in it. Several details below come from search snippets and a summarizing fetch tool, not from reading the raw spec, and are marked unverified.
data_model:
VTK in-memory model: Points (N x 3), cells as connectivity plus offsets (vtkCellArray, offsets array of length ncells+1) plus a per-cell type id (e.g. VTK_POLYHEDRON = 42; the number 42 comes from a vtkusers post and from memory, so unverified against the type table). There is no explicit edge or face entity for ordinary cells. Faces and edges are derived on the fly, and only polyhedra carry explicit faces.

VTKHDF UnstructuredGrid (spec 2.8): the root group /VTKHDF has attributes Version (2 ints) and Type ("UnstructuredGrid"). Datasets are Points, Connectivity, Offsets, Types, and the per-partition size arrays NumberOfPoints, NumberOfCells and NumberOfConnectivityIds (length = number of partitions). Offsets has NumberOfCells[i]+1 entries per partition (sum of S(i)+1). Arrays live in PointData/, CellData/ and FieldData/. Each array may carry an Attribute attribute (Scalars, Normals, GlobalIds, HigherOrderDegrees, and others). The spec says the dtypes are fixed at write time and not tabulated. Source: https://docs.vtk.org/en/latest/vtk_file_formats/vtkhdf_file_format/vtkhdf_specifications.html

Polyhedra in VTKHDF (added in spec 2.5): datasets FaceConnectivity and FaceOffsets (faces as polygons, which may be shared between polyhedra), PolyhedronToFaces (face ids per polyhedron), PolyhedronOffsets (one entry per cell, repeating the previous value for non-polyhedral cells, so face count = next minus current), plus the metadata arrays NumberOfFaces, NumberOfPolyhedronToFaceIds and NumberOfFaceConnectivityIds.
